claims.claim: A property management system (PMS) is the core operational software of a lodging business, holding reservations, room status, check-in/out records, billing/folios, and coordinating housekeeping and reporting, and it functions as the central hub that other systems integrate with.
A point-of-sale (POS) system records sales at outlets such as restaurants and shops and can post a guest's room charge directly to the PMS folio through an interface, so it appears on the final bill.

A central reservation system (CRS) is a computerized system that stores a hotel's availability, rates, and inventory and manages bookings across channels, and it often serves as the reservation core the PMS works from.

A channel manager collects availability and rates from the CRS or PMS and distributes them to channels such as GDSs, OTAs, metasearch sites, and the hotel website, then feeds bookings back, updating all channels when a room sells to prevent double-selling.

A global distribution system (GDS) is a network, originating in the airline industry's computerized reservation systems, that connects hotels to travel agents and corporate travel buyers; an online travel agency (OTA) is a consumer-facing marketplace where travelers book directly.
In one open educational source, OTAs accounted for roughly 24 percent of transient reservations in North American markets in 2020.

Systems in the stack exchange data through interfaces and application programming interfaces (APIs); a two-way integration lets a booking flow from a channel into the CRS/PMS while the availability change flows back out, keeping one reservation consistent across systems.

A revenue management system (RMS) analyzes demand and market conditions to recommend pricing and inventory controls, and a CRM system aggregates guest profiles and history; the PMS integrates with both.
Modern PMS platforms support guest-facing technology such as contactless check-in and checkout via tablet kiosks or mobile apps.

The PCI Security Standards Council, founded by the major payment brands, develops the PCI Data Security Standard (PCI DSS) to protect payment-account data; the standard applies to entities that store, process, or transmit payment-account data, and whether an entity must validate compliance is set by payment brands or acquirers rather than the Council.

U.S. FTC guidance for businesses summarizes core data-security practices: collect only the personal data you need, control access to it, require secure authentication, store and transmit sensitive data securely (including encryption), segment and monitor networks, and dispose of data no longer needed.
